analysis.one_liner: Moves Medicare's drug price negotiations and lower out-of-pocket caps forward by two years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have started Medicare drug price negotiations in 2024 instead of 2026, never got a committee hearing or a vote and ended the Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Medicare won't negotiate prices directly with drug makers for the first batch of expensive drugs until 2026, and the new $2,000 out-of-pocket cap for Medicare drug plans doesn't start until 2025. This bill moves both up by two years, so seniors would pay less sooner. It sat in two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with high prescription drug costs. They would hit the annual out-of-pocket cap earlier and would see Medicare-negotiated prices on the first round of expensive drugs in 2024 rather than 2026 [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It moves the annual out-of-pocket threshold changes for the Medicare drug benefit forward one year, so beneficiaries reach the point where they pay little or nothing for drugs sooner [S2].

It moves the Medicare drug price negotiation program up two years: negotiated prices for the first group of drugs would take effect in 2024 instead of 2026, with each following year's group moved up two years as well [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face Medicare-negotiated lower prices two years earlier and sooner exposure to the Part D benefit redesign; Medicare drug plans would also have to adjust to the accelerated benefit changes [S2].

drawbacks.text: The accelerated timeline was likely not workable as written: the negotiation program's first cycle required drug selection in 2023 and months of negotiation before 2026 prices, and drug prices for 2024 could not realistically have been negotiated after the fact [S2].
Moving the Part D benefit redesign up a year would have disrupted plan-year pricing already set by Medicare drug plans for 2024, creating administrative and operational strain [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — seniors paying less for prescription drugs two years sooner — is broadly popular, but the bill as drafted pushed the negotiation timeline back retroactively in a way that insurers and drug makers would have struggled to execute. A more workable acceleration, or the 2024 Part D redesign disruption it ignored, would be the strongest honest objection. On paper the benefit to seniors outweighs the administrative cost; the bill's real problem was that it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to two House committees, and sent to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Seth Magaziner introduced the bill on October 11, 2023 [S1].
On October 25, 2023 it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, first in November 2023 and again in December 2024, and never advanced to a full committee vote or the House floor [S4].
The bill ended the 118th Congress with zero cosponsors [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which avoided two years of earlier Medicare-negotiated prices and the accelerated Part D cost-sharing changes. Medicare beneficiaries did not get the earlier savings the bill promised.

for.name: Rep. Seth Magaziner
for.role: U.S. Representative, Rhode Island; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to accelerate Medicare's drug price negotiation program and the Part D out-of-pocket cap changes.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of first referral; chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred here and to its Health Subcommittee, where it received no hearing or markup in either 2023 or its December 2024 re-referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Second committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred here for its Medicare provisions; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the sole sponsor was a Democrat with zero cosponsors, including from his own party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have forced Medicare-negotiated lower prices to take effect in 2024 instead of 2026 and sped up the Part D redesign that shifts more drug costs off seniors, cutting manufacturer revenue sooner. Their interest in the bill's failure ran directly against seniors' interest in cheaper drugs.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurance plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill would have accelerated the Part D benefit redesign a year, disrupting plan pricing and increasing plans' share of drug costs under the redesign, while beneficiaries reached their out-of-pocket cap sooner. Plans had no role in the bill's consideration.
